707639.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʰepʰəlā́, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-l̥ (“head”) + *-éh₂ (“nominal suffix”). Compare κεβλή (keblḗ).

707612.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kenwós, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱen-. Cognates with Old Armenian սին (sin, “vain, trifling”).

707666.t: Uncertain. Possibilities include: * Metathesized from the Semitic root כ־ד־ב (k-ḏ-b) / ك ذ ب (k ḏ b) (Hebrew כ־ז־ב (k-z-b)) related to lies.

707616.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kéntron, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱéntrom, from *ḱent- (“to prick; point”); direct cognate with Albanian çandër (“forked pole”) and probably Old Armenian սանտր (santr), սանդր (sandr, “comb”).

707625.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kérats, probably remodeled from an earlier s-stem *kéras (like κάρα (kắrā), κάρηνον (kắrēnon), κρανίον (krāníon)), as preserved in e.g. κερασ-φόρος (keras-phóros, “with a horn”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head, top; front of…

707669.t: According to Beekes, acquired from Pre-Greek. Said Pre-Greek term may be ultimately derived from or at least related to Proto-Hurro-Urartian *kinnar (“lyre, harp”).

707659.t: A foreign loan from a substrate language, cognate with Latin cēra and Albanian qiri, and possibly also with Lithuanian korys, Latvian kāre.

707646.t: From κηδεύω (kēdeúō, “to care for”) + -εία (-eíā). The sense of "care for the dead" > "funeral" developed in the Hellenistic Koine era.

707679.t: From Proto-Indo-European *keyh₂- (“to start to move”). Compare κίω (kĭ́ō, “to go”) and κίνυμαι (kī́nŭmai, “to go; move”), Latin cieō (“to move”).

707678.t: The connection with κίνδαξ (kíndax, “quick, nimble”), ὀνοκίνδιος (onokíndios, “donkey-driver”) is formally attractive.

707619.t: From κέραμος (kérămos, “pottery”) + -εύς (-eús, suffix for person concerned). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀐𐀨𐀕𐀄 (ke-ra-me-u /⁠kerameus⁠/, “potter”).

707631.t: Thematic transformation of an r/n stem *κεραϝαρ (*kerawar) (< Proto-Hellenic *kerawər), from a verb "to shatter" that was replaced by the related κεραΐζω (keraḯzō), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“to smash, shatter”).

707662.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kārūt͏̌t͏̌ō. By surface analysis, κήρυκ- (kḗrūk-, stem of κῆρυξ (kêrŭx)) + *-ϳω (*-jō).

707667.t: From an original *τῖβωτός (*tîbōtós), from Aramaic תֵּיבוֹתָא (tēḇōṯā), from a merger of Egyptian DbA-b-t:pr (ḏbꜣt, “sarcophagus, coffin”) and d-b-t:xt (dbt, “chest, box”), as also synonymous Arabic تَابُوت (tābūt) and Hebrew תֵּבָה (tēḇā́).

707622.t: Unknown. Has long been compared to κεράννυμι (keránnumi, “to mix”), but could also be related to Latin cremō, Proto-West Germanic *herþ (English hearth), or Sanskrit कूडयति (kūḍayati, “to burn, scorch”).

707661.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *káruks. Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀏𐀬𐀏 (ka-ru-ka, accusative singular).

707654.t: From Proto-Indo-European *keh₂po-s (“land, garden”), which seems to be from *kap- (“to seize”) (though Beekes is skeptical of this relation and tentatively separates the two).

707684.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew כִּנּוֹר (kinnōr) and adapted to κινυρός (kinurós, “wailing”).

707653.t: Unexplained. The connection with Old Armenian քամեմ (kʻamem, “to press (out)”) is formally possible but it is incompatible with the probable basic meaning of the Greek word, wicker.

707652.t: The formation is like κνημίς (knēmī́s, “greave”). A comparable meaning can be found in Latin calidus (“with a bless on the head”).

707693.t: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek. Furnée compares κιθάρα (kĭthắrā, “ivy”).

707683.t: According to Herodotus, from Phoenician; compare Hebrew קִנָּמוֹן (kinamón, “cinnamon”). The ending was modelled on that of ἄμωμον (ắmōmon, “black cardamom”), or due to folk etymology, on that of ἄμωμος (ắmōmos, “blameless”).

707660.t: From *κήρυγϳ- (*kḗrūgj-, stem of κηρύσσω (kērū́ssō, “to proclaim”)) + -μα (-mă, result noun suffix), from κήρυκ- (kḗrūk-, stem of κῆρυξ (kêrŭx, “herald”)).
